method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Combining anticholinergic medicines** can cause agitated delirium, dilated pupils, dry mouth and tachycardia.
claims.source_text: Many medications may have anticholinergic effects and interaction between two or more of these medications can lead to symptoms such as an agitated delirium, mydriasis, dry mouth and tachycardia
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Serious features are seizures, coma and cardiac conduction abnormalities.** **Delirium can persist for days** after an acute ingestion.
claims.source_text: Serious symptoms include seizures, coma and cardiac conduction abnormalities and resolution of symptoms can be variable - delirium can persist for days following an acute ingestion
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If you suspect it, get senior advice and discuss with a toxicologist.** For 24-hour advice, call the Victorian Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.
claims.source_text: If anticholinergic syndrome is suspected please seek senior advice and discuss with toxicologist. … For 24 hour advice, contact the Victorian Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Polypharmacy overdoses can hide the anticholinergic pattern.** Seizures, coma and cardiovascular toxicity may come from effects at other receptors, not muscarinic ones.
claims.source_text: seizures, coma and cardiovascular toxicity may not be mediated by muscarinic effects, rather secondary to drug effects at other receptors, as many anticholinergic medications are active at numerous receptors / ion channels. Polypharmacy overdoses may make the anticholinergic toxidrome less apparent.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Standard doses can be enough in susceptible children:** infants, children with Trisomy 21 or spastic paralysis, and blond/blue-eyed children.
claims.source_text: increased susceptibility to standard doses of anticholinergics (more common in infants, children with Trisomy 21, spastic paralysis and blond/blue-eyed children)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Common culprits:** antihistamines (diphenhydramine, doxylamine, promethazine, chlorpheniramine, cyproheptadine) · dextromethorphan · tricyclic antidepressants · antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, droperidol, haloperidol, quetiapine, olanzapine) · carbamazepine · hyoscine · cyclopentolate and homatropine eye drops · plants such as Angel's Trumpet/Datura · oxybutynin, benztropine, glycopyrrolate.
claims.source_text: Anti-histamines Diphenhydramine, Doxylamine, Promethazine, Chlorpheniramine, Cyproheptadine Anti-tussives Dextromethorphan Antidepressants Tricyclic antidepressants (Amitriptyline, Imipramine, Doxepin) Anti-psychotics Chlorpromazine, Droperidol, Haloperidol, Quetiapine, Olanzapine Anti-convulsants Carbamazepine Anti-emetics/travel sickness Hyoscine (scopolamine) Topical ophthalmoplegics Cyclopentolate, Homatropine Plants Deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna), jimsonweed, mandrake root, lupin beans, Angel's Trumpet / Datura … Other Oxybutynin, benztropine, glycopyrrolate
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Assess:** any symptomatic child, and every child or young person with intentional self-poisoning or a significant accidental ingestion.
claims.source_text: Children requiring Assessment Any symptomatic child All children or young person with intentional self-poisoning or significant accidental ingestion
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Central sign: agitated delirium** — restlessness or violence, visual hallucinations, picking at imaginary objects, mumbling or slurred speech, fluctuating mental state.
claims.source_text: The characteristic feature of toxicity at central receptors is agitated delirium. This may include: Restlessness / fidgeting /violent behaviour Visual hallucinations Picking at imaginary objects in the air or on the bedsheets Mumbling / slurred speech Fluctuating mental status
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mnemonic:** hot as a hare (fever) · red as a beet (flushed skin) · blind as a bat (dilated pupils) · dry as a bone (dry mouth and eyes, less sweating) · mad as a hatter (delirium) · full as a flask (urinary retention). Severity is generally dose dependent.
claims.source_text: "Hot as a hare": Fever "Red as a beet:" Flushed skin "Blind as a bat": Mydriasis "Dry as a bone": Dry mouth, dry eyes and decreased sweating "Mad as a hatter": Delirium … Urinary retention The severity of symptoms and signs is generally dose dependent.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider the look-alikes:** serotonin syndrome, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, salicylate toxicity; and non-toxic causes such as encephalitis, sepsis, neurotrauma, post-ictal states, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia.
claims.source_text: Other toxicological syndromes such as: Serotonin syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Malignant hyperthermia Salicylate toxicity Non-toxicological causes may include: Encephalitis Sepsis Neurotrauma Post-ictal phenomena Hypoglycaemia Hyponatraemia Behavioural disturbance
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Deliberate self-poisoning: 12-lead ECG, blood glucose and paracetamol level.** Some cough medicines contain paracetamol, so consider a level in accidental ingestions too.
claims.source_text: Screening tests - 12 lead ECG, blood glucose and paracetamol concentration - in deliberate self-poisoning. … Some cough medications may also contain paracetamol - so a concentration should be considered in these accidental ingestions as well.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider** salicylate level if salicylate toxicity is on the differential, specific drug levels (eg carbamazepine), UEC and CK.
claims.source_text: Consider salicylate concentrations if differential includes salicylate toxicity. … Consider concentrations for specific agents if available - eg carbamazepine Consider UEC and CK
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stop the causative agents.** Active resuscitation is rarely needed. **Hypotension: start with a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus.**
claims.source_text: Stop any causative agents Active resuscitation is infrequently required. … Hypotension should be addressed initially with a 20 ml/kg crystalloid bolus.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Seizures: benzodiazepines.** Treat hypoglycaemia. ⚠️ **Hyperthermia: cool the child — antipyretics don't help.**
claims.source_text: Treat seizures with benzodiazepines Treat hypoglycaemia Treat hyperthermia with cooling measures. Antipyretics are unhelpful.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mild cases:** reassurance and a quiet area may be enough; 1-to-1 nursing often helps.
claims.source_text: Reassurance and management in a quiet area may be sufficient for those with mild signs/symptoms. These children often benefit from 1-to-1 nursing.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Agitation/delirium: diazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 5–10 mg), oral every 30 minutes or IV every 15 minutes, titrated until resting but rousable.** **Avoid haloperidol and droperidol** — they can worsen anticholinergic effects.
claims.source_text: Agitation / delirium is typically managed with titrated diazepam (0.1 mg/kg - to a max of 5-10 mg) PO every 30 minutes or every 15 minutes IV until the child is resting but able to be roused. Avoid haloperidol and droperidol, which may worsen anticholinergic effects.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Urinary retention can drive agitation** — a bladder scan shows whether a catheter is needed.
claims.source_text: Urinary retention may contribute to the agitation. Bladder scan will reveal the need for a urinary catheter.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Decontamination and enhanced elimination depend on the drug** — discuss with a toxicologist. **Physostigmine is controversial**; use it only after discussion with toxicology.
claims.source_text: The use of decontamination / enhanced elimination depend on the actual medication exposure, and should be discussed with a toxicologist. … There exists some controversy over the use of physostigmine - a cholinesterase inhibitor - which has been used to reduce delirium in anticholinergic syndrome. The use of physostigmine may be indicated following discussion with the toxicology service.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Admit symptomatic children** for monitoring and treatment. **Transfer** when care is beyond the hospital's comfort level — PIPER 1300 137 650.
claims.source_text: Symptomatic children require admission for monitoring and treatment if necessary … Children requiring care beyond the comfort level of the current hospital For emergency advice and paediatric or neonatal ICU transfers, call the Paediatric Infant Perinatal Emergency Retrieval (PIPER) Service: 1300 137 650.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Observe asymptomatic at-risk children for 6 hours.** **Discharge needs a normal GCS, a normal ECG and a safe discharge plan**; after deliberate ingestion, a risk assessment showing low risk of further self-harm.
claims.source_text: Asymptomatic children at risk of anticholinergic syndrome - with deliberate self-poisoning or significant accidental ingestion should be observed for 6 hours. … Prior to discharge, all children require: Normal GCS Normal ECG Ensure provision for safe discharge are in place In cases of deliberate ingestion, a risk assessment should indicate that the child or young person is at low risk of further self harm in the discharge setting.
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Anticholinergic syndrome' (Last updated August 2017), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Anticholinergic_syndrome/, retrieved 2026-09-23
